Action agenda

Many issues that were intensely negotiated at COP31 – including the electrification goal and fossil-fuel phaseout – also featured in the “action agenda”.

This is the part of the UN climate process that involves mobilising real-world climate action from non-state actors, including businesses, investors and civil-society groups. 

It also covers voluntary actions taken by groups of countries beyond the COP negotiations.

When the “Antalya pact” failed to materialise, the presidency’s action agenda package was one of its more substantial outputs. 

In this closing remarks at COP31, after the headline negotiated outcome had collapsed, UNFCCC executive secretary Simon Stiell reminded delegates:

“This COP process has two tracks. And across the action agenda, COP31 has delivered real progress and concrete results.”

With Australia overseeing negotiations, the action agenda was instead a priority for the Turkish presidency, which used COP31 to launch a variety of new projects and “compacts”.

In a phrase familiar to attendees of previous COPs, Turkish COP31 president Murat Kurum said he wanted an “implementation COP” that would leave people saying: “Something changed in Antalya.”

Amid global conflict, struggling multilateralism and the imminent breaching of the 1.5C Paris Agreement goal, UN climate talks have repeatedly failed to reach consensus on vital issues.

Some have, therefore, welcomed what the Brazilian COP30 presidency called “two-tier multilateralism”, in which parties try to find consensus where they can and, where they cannot, coalitions of willing nations and groups push more ambitious action forward.

Kaveh Guilanpour, vice president for international strategies at the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES), told Carbon Brief:

“There’s a lot of inertia in the formal way of negotiating and we’re trying to find our way to whatever that new thing is, given the foundational era of negotiations is over.”

Last year, the Brazilian presidency consolidated hundreds of existing climate initiatives – including many launched at previous COPs – into a streamlined set that could be supported and tracked under the action agenda.

This included setting out more than 120 “plans to accelerate solutions”, to advance everything from phasing out coal to ending food waste. Tracking by UN Climate Change found that 104 of these plans had seen progress over the past year.

By the end of COP31, the total number of plans had increased to 136, with new ones filling “important gaps”, such as early warning systems.

Crucially, the plans were structured to align with the global stocktake outcomes from COP28 – such as curbing fossil fuels and tripling renewables – which all nations agreed on. 

In this way, the revised action agenda is intended to explicitly support negotiated outcomes.

Turkey announced 10 “priority themes” for the COP31 action agenda, fitting them into the existing framework. By far the most high profile was the “electrification” focus. (See: Electrification.)

A book distributed at the summit by the Turkish presidency stated that a “large number of events, declarations and partnerships does not by itself constitute implementation success”.

Nevertheless, the presidency did launch many new initiatives, including six voluntary 2035 targets that countries and non-state actors could sign up for. 

These included “compacts” to curb the “energy intensity” of buildings by 25% and increase the use of “circular materials” in manufacturing to at least 15% by 2035. These initiatives attracted dozens of backers, but gained far less support than the electrification goal.

Other notable initiatives pushed by the Turkish presidency include a domestic pledge for “zero waste districts” and an “Antalya artificial intelligence (AI) pledge”, which focused on curbing data-centre emissions while advancing “AI solutions for climate action”.

COP31 also saw progress on two initiatives launched by COP30’s “global mutirão” decision that are relevant for the growth of the action agenda. The first was the “Belém mission to 1.5”, which identified key priority areas for countries to meet their climate goals. 

The second was the “global implementation accelerator”, which was formally established at COP31. This involves presidencies and experts choosing two action-agenda plans each year that are best placed to drive “positive tipping points” for climate action. 

Cosima Cassel, E3G climate diplomacy lead, told Carbon Brief that this focus, “based on science, not just on the presidency’s priorities…is an extra step in the evolution of the action agenda”.

During a COP31 session on the “accelerator”, COP30 strategy director Túlio Andrade said the Brazilian team wanted it to advance the transition “from a negotiation-focused regime to one very much focused on implementation”.

The Turkish presidency also announced a new project called the “climate implementation bridge”, while pledging an initial $3m to support its operations.

In partnership with the UN Development Programme, the bridge’s goal is to turn nations’ climate plans into “bankable projects” and connect them with finance. 

Together, the “mission”, “accelerator” and “bridge” form part of a wider “ecosystem” that supporters hope will identify and support priority areas of climate action.

However, the growing profile of the action agenda has resulted in pushback, with India and the Arab group arguing against any mention of it in formal negotiations. In contrast, Brazil accused the presidency of failing to significantly acknowledge these “concrete instruments and initiatives” in the proposed “Antalya pact”. 

Some parties and observers are concerned that the action agenda is a diversion from parties’ obligations under UN climate treaties, such as providing climate finance.

Arguing that the focus should instead be on reforming the COP process, Vanuatu climate minister Ralph Regenvanu told Carbon Brief:

“Unfortunately, the action agenda has not necessarily led to action. It is indicative, again, that the COP process is broken. While people innovating and coming together to take action is good, it cannot take the place of negotiations.”

Developing countries, which often have far fewer delegates, also struggle to follow all the additional activities. In a closing session, Stiell invited parties to nominate focal points so that the UN could help to “connect them with action agenda opportunities all year round”.

Guilanpour noted that while “everybody says they want to focus on implementation”, within the traditional COP process this can only apply to “a very rarefied subset of obligations”, such as submitting revised NDCs. He added:

“When the rest of the world hears implementation, they want to see pollution in their city going down, their energy bills going down…and that sort of implementation is in the action agenda.”

Global leaders

COP31’s world leaders’ summit took place during the conference’s first week from 11-12 November.

Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva – whose recent re-election was widely interpreted as a timely boost for climate action and multilateralism by delegates – gave a blistering speech in the summit’s opening ceremony. He told other world leaders:

“We have started talking more about weapons and tariffs than about the survival of future generations…But the planet cannot be left at the mercy of hegemonic disputes.”

He told leaders that he wanted COP30, which took place last year in the Brazilian city of Belém, to be remembered as the “COP of truth” – but that “science and multilateralism remain under attack”, adding:

“It is not by chance that the incorporation of IPCC contributions into the COP negotiation process is in question. Nor is it a coincidence that climate agreements are the favourite targets of reactionary forces at COPs.”

He also touted Brazil’s newly released global roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation, urging COP31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia to “ensure that the recommendations contained in these documents are disseminated and incorporated into the next global stocktake”.

In one of his final addresses in the role, UN secretary general António Guterres said that the “brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us”, adding:

“Leaders – and, in particular, those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil-fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C.”

Turkish leader Recep Tayyip Erdoğan used his address to call on developed countries to “take greater responsibility for emission reductions and financing” and to call out “ecocide” in Gaza.

(Erdoğan faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields in Turkey on the eve of the summit.)

Barbados prime minister Mia Mottley cited Carbon Brief analysis to reprimand developed countries in her address to the world leaders’ summit, telling the room:

”My friends, let us be clear: pledges are not payments. But even the promised pledges are now 70% below previous levels.”

UK prime minister Andy Burnham, the only G7 leader to attend the summit, said that electrification is “how we make clean power cheap power”. He also announced the appointment of the country’s first special representative on climate security. 

In total, around 70 world leaders spoke at the summit – with many major polluters missing.

For the second year, the US did not send any delegates to COP. (Donald Trump took the US out of the Paris Agreement and the UN climate treaty after returning to office.)

However, success for Democrats in the US midterm elections, shortly before COP31, lifted hopes that the world’s second-largest emitter could one day return to the talks.

“America is all in” – a coalition of mostly Democratic governors, Congress members and local mayors – had a pavilion at COP31 and brought around 120 delegates (a figure larger than many official country delegations).

Speaking on 16 November at a pavilion event attended by Carbon Brief, Jared Huffman, a Democratic Congressional representative from California, said that the midterm results were a “clear rejection” of Trump’s “climate denial” and “wrecking ball to climate and energy policy”. He added:

“The next time that we are here at a COP, it will be different…We will be an official Congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives. And soon after that, this yellow part of our lanyard that says ‘observer’ will change and the US will truly be officially back in as part of the negotiati[ons].”

Other countries without delegations at the talks included Myanmar and Israel, according to Carbon Brief analysis.

More than 92,000 registered for COP, making it potentially the largest in history, found Carbon Brief analysis.

Electrification

Amid a global energy crisis driven by disruption in the trade of fossil fuels, one of the biggest themes of COP31 was electrification. 

Much attention was focused on which nations had signed up to a voluntary pledge to “increase the share of electricity in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035”. 

For much of COP31, this was expected to be one of the main outcomes in the “Antalya pact” cover text, which ultimately failed to find agreement among parties. (See: Cover decision.)

Nevertheless, some countries made public pledges of support for the target during the COP, including in a joint China-Australia statement. 

COP31 president Murat Kurum told the closing plenary that “around 80” countries were behind the goal, but a full list was never published.

The pledge was launched earlier in the year as a “flagship initiative of the COP31 presidency’s action agenda” – part of its wider goal to “electrify the world”. (See: Action agenda.)

As explained on CB Connect, it drew from analysis by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), which was explicitly designed to align with the 1.5C target and support the Brazilian COP30 presidency’s “roadmap” for transitioning away from fossil fuels. 

Towards the end of COP31, the presidency launched its “electrification delivery package”, capturing 14 newly announced international initiatives and other relevant projects.

Among them were an industry-backed “maritime electrification goal” to increase electricity’s share of shipping’s final energy demand to 20% by 2035, as well as projects to boost grid investment, renewables in small-island states and transitions away from coal.

One notable initiative was the Electrify Now Finance Coalition – launched with the backing of the COP31 and COP32 presidencies – to “mobilise over $1.2bn for clean electrification projects” in developing countries.

At a coalition launch event, featuring ministers from Ethiopia, Germany, Pakistan and several other nations, Bruce Douglas, chief executive of the Global Renewables Alliance, told attendees that at least 25 nations had already put in place policies to drive electrification since the start of the “Hormuz crisis”. He said:

“We now have the formula for success: renewable energy plus electrification equals secure, affordable and clean energy for all consumers.”

China at COP31

Closing COP31 with a signal of “solidarity and multilateralism” was “more important than specific problems”, said China at the opening plenary of the summit.

Its climate officials said repeatedly that not every COP required a “new outcome” and noted the need to “manage expectations”. 

These comments seemed prescient when negotiations broke down at the end of COP31 over the cover decision.

China had outlined its key aims for COP31 in a press conference held by Li Gao, vice-minister of ecology and environment and delegation head, in late October.

These were primarily to commit developed countries to do more on mitigation and finance, as well as to address “unilateralism and protectionism” in the trade of clean-energy technologies.

But Li also “commend[ed]” the presidency’s call for countries to pledge to achieve a 35% share of electricity in global final energy consumption by 2035.

One of the biggest questions hovering over the COP was whether China would officially support the pledge, which was incorporated into the failed cover text. 

While observers had told Carbon Brief from early in the negotiations that it would be very likely that China would support the pledge in some form, the strongest signal came from a joint statement published with Australia in the second week.

In it, the two countries “welcome[d] growing international ambition and cooperation on electrification…on a voluntary basis”, mentioning the 35 by 35 goal, as well as recognising various climate, social and economic benefits from the transition. (See: Electrification.) 

The cover text had similarly sought to “recognise that electrification has significant benefits in terms of emission reductions, energy security, energy efficiency, economic development and energy access”.

The joint statement, however, did not explicitly mention fossil fuels, rather it noted “countries have different transition pathways” and the “importance of secure, affordable, reliable and resilient energy systems during the transition”.

Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), told Carbon Brief that the “carefully curated” language helped “firm up” support for the electrification pledge – and broader language around energy – in the final draft. 

China had published a joint climate statement with the EU ahead of COP30, as well as ones with the US ahead of COPs including COP21, COP26 and COP28.

But, unlike these agreements, the Australia-China joint statement “mostly confirms existing relatively unambitious negotiation points and does not advance ambitions” on issues including fossil fuels and decarbonising trade, argued Prof Christoph Nedopil Wang at the University of Queensland.

He told Carbon Brief: “Symbolically, it would have been more meaningful to sign a more ambitious statement before COP negotiations began.”

As talks broke down at the closing plenary, China endorsed the cover text’s final draft, noting that, although it has “some concerns about the content”, it chose to accept the decision to “push forward our process and show a message of unity and collective efforts”.

On 23 November, China’s foreign ministry issued a statement saying: 

“We express our disappointment regarding this outcome, but believe that confidence in the multilateral process should not be lost as a result.”

“China was not the main blocker for the text”, said ASPI’s Li. 

He added that, in his view, even if language around transitioning away from fossil fuels had been made stronger, China would have found it acceptable.

China also tried to preserve the mitigation work programme (MWP) at the closing plenary. (See: Mitigation work programme.) 

In negotiations, China joined other developing countries in supporting the work programme’s extension through to 2030. 

Speaking on behalf of the LMDCs, China emphasised the value of the MWP, but said it needed to “focus on how to eliminate barriers of implementation”, according to Third World Network. 

These included developed countries’ lack of mitigation action and financial support, as well as unilateral trade measures, it added. 

China, on behalf of the LMDCs, tried to build consensus around the MWP at the closing plenary by suggesting deleting references to the first global stocktake. However, the suggestion was rejected by Russia.

Meanwhile, China continued to emphasise the need for a gradual transition away from fossil fuels throughout the COP.

“‘Phasing out fossil fuels’ [淘汰化石燃料] is merely a proposition of a small number of countries and has never constituted a consensus”, climate envoy Liu Zhenmin told the Paper. 

He added that the energy transition required “gradually replacing fossil fuels” with clean energy over the course of “decades” and that phasing out fossil fuels should not “become a focal point of COP31 negotiations”.

A few days later and thousands of miles away, the presidents of China, the US and Russia declared at the APEC Summit that the three countries “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products” in response to global energy shocks. The China delegation office at COP31 did not respond to Carbon Brief’s request for comment on this matter. 

An early push to get trade on the agenda came not from China, but from the African group. In the end, the item was not included on the agenda, though it was raised by China in negotiations on the just transition work programme, adaptation fund and standing committee on finance.

The China-Australia joint statement notes “measures taken to combat climate change should not constitute a means of arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination or a disguised restriction on international trade”.

Prof Nedopil Wang told Carbon Brief that Australia would be more open to compromise on language with China around cleantech trade than the EU or US, as its economy has few “domestic substitutes for China’s manufactured products”.

Text on trade measures were included in the cover decision drafts, though not adopted by parties.

China did also focus significant attention on the just transition work programme, which was successfully passed. (See: Just transition work programme.)

Speaking at a ministerial roundtable, environment vice-minister Li said that the “just transition is one of the most important agenda items of COP31” and must be operationalised. 

In negotiations, China called for the mechanism to recognise the “north-south development gap” and a dedicated body to manage the programme – opposed by the EU.

More broadly, the LMDCs urged that the work programme “avoid policy prescriptions” and not be linked to the global stocktake, which they argued would risk creating new obligations.

Meanwhile, at a high-level dialogue on climate finance, watched by Carbon Brief, environment minister Huang Runqiu said that developed countries’ “climate finance commitments must be honoured and the financing gap narrowed”.

Huang called for the new collective quantified goal (NCQG) to be “effectively implemented”, as well as for “establishing a common definition” for climate finance and improving accounting methodologies. 

He additionally highlighted the need to improve the “quality of finance”, such as providing more grants and highly concessional loans, support for adaptation and easier access to climate finance.

This was echoed by BASIC, who said that “developed countries must set a pathway towards the NCQG goal of $300bn annually” and triple adaptation finance. BASIC also said the climate finance work programme (CFWP) must “operationalise Article 9.1”.

The final CFWP text was passed, but only focused on procedural matters, with mentions of tripling adaptation finance and “burden-sharing” in earlier drafts removed. Requests to expand the donor base were also deleted.

China maintained its emphasis on Article 9.1 in a number of workstreams, notably through the CFWP and standing committee on finance.

Carbon Brief understands that China was also one of two nations driving efforts to ensure that a dialogue on Article 2.1(c), which ensures finance flows are “consistent” with climate action, remains open and non-binding.

On adaptation finance, China underscored on behalf of the LMDCs the need to triple funds, calling for a “clear roadmap and timeline to increase the share of grants, as well as a progress-review mechanism”, said Third World Network.

But, in general, ASPI’s Li says, “China’s position was right in the middle of the political spectrum” on most of the issues being negotiated, maintaining a “quiet, but self-assured posture”.

An early point of discussion among delegates had been whether China could have signalled greater leadership at COP, such as by announcing a bid to host COP33.

News emerged at COP31 that China had, after “months” of consideration, decided not to do so. 

Prof Hu Bin, associate professor and director of global climate governance research at Tsinghua University’s Institute of Climate Change and Sustainable Development, told Carbon Brief that “China, politically, is still very hesitant” to claim the role of the leading country on climate. Instead it is focusing on leading in terms of the transition on-the-ground he said, adding:

“I still think the reason China doesn’t want to bid for COP33 is internal pressure – the economy is slowing down, local governments are facing lots of pressure for employment and for economic growth.” 

Another way in which it was suggested China could display leadership was by helping create consensus around the IPCC’s AR7 report being published in time for the second global stocktake. 

At an event at the China pavilion attended by Carbon Brief, Laurence Tubiana, key architect of the Paris Agreement, said she will “count on China to be the torchbearer for the world’s science at the second global stocktake”.

But, at the same event, Prof Wang Yi argued that IPCC reports from AR1 to AR6 were “unequivocal that global warming is caused by human activity”. Wang is a professor at the Chinese Academy of Science and a lead advisor to the China delegation.

This means the science is clear, “no matter” when AR7 is published, he added.

China instead continued to position itself as a champion of the global south, both in negotiations and around the COP.

In negotiations, it consistently aligned itself with developing country parties and groups, calling for solutions that would not “widen” the north-south gap.

South-south cooperation was the subject of a high-level forum at which China’s vice-president Han Zheng spoke. 

Han emphasised that “China will vigorously deepen south-south cooperation” and formally announced a new global south climate leadership training programme, according to a recording of the speech obtained by Carbon Brief.

China also signed an agreement with Turkey to invest $15bn in developing 7GW of solar and wind power and 4GW of transmission capacity.

This deal “could be seen as part of China’s own contribution to climate finance and accelerating the global energy transition”, even if it’s not “formally accounted”, said Kate Logan, director of the China Climate Hub and climate diplomacy at ASPI. 

She added that, at a broader level, it shows that “China will continue exercising its influence through real-economy actions, even while its negotiators press for developed country accountability on finance”.

Ocean

Ocean advocates had several outcomes to celebrate at COP31 – and also some disappointment.

Before the summit started, observers – and many parties – were hopeful of securing a strong outcome for the ocean, especially in light of the pre-COP meeting held in Pacific island states.

A letter sent to the COP31 presidencies on 8 October – signed by the African group, the EU (along with its member states) and 24 other countries – called for the COP to “move sustainable ocean-based climate action from recognition to implementation”. 

It said that such a move should be “backed by a clear political signal, a coherent plan for integration into the Paris Agreement ambition cycle and its existing means of implementation”.

Analysis published by the World Resources Institute (WRI) on 15 November found that 95% of coastal and island countries included “at least one ocean-based action” in their national climate plans. However, it added that “more than 60% of ocean-commitment implementation depends on receiving some form of external support.”

Two days later, on the “ocean, seas, nature and land use” thematic day, ministers from France and Brazil announced the launch of the “Blue NDC Challenge implementation task force” at a side event. They also welcomed 10 new countries as members of the Blue NDC Challenge – a group launched at the UN Ocean Conference in Nice, France, in June 2025 to “advance ocean-based climate action”.

The same day, the COP31 presidency published the “Antalya Ocean and Seas Compact”, a high-level declaration that it said drew on feedback from parties and discussions at several events, including the UN General Assembly and the Pacific pre-COP. 

The document highlights the impacts of climate change on the ocean, recognises the ocean’s importance in climate action and invites parties to strengthen their ocean work.

Dr Tom Pickerell, global ocean programme director at WRI, told Carbon Brief:

“It was more of a platform for collective ambition and political alignment, rather than any targets or finance coming through. We wouldn’t say no to it, but if we’d left just with that, it would have been a little bit sad.”

Also on the ocean thematic day, the UK government announced a new £20m ($26.2m) funding commitment to marine protection. This comprised £11.8m ($15.5m) to the Global Fund for Coral Reefs and £9m ($11.8m) to the Global Ocean Accounts Partnership, which helps countries measure their progress towards sustainable ocean development.

Towards the end of the summit, the “high-level climate-resilient coral reef commitment” gained six new signatories: Colombia, Haiti, Jamaica, Niue, Samoa and Tuvalu. These governments “commit to protect[ing] reefs identified as having greater potential to persist through climate change”, according to a press release announcing the new countries.

In the formal negotiation rooms, ocean groups were closely following discussions around the cover decision, hoping to see the ocean featured prominently there. (See: Cover decision.)

Draft versions of the cover text “invite[d]” the development of a multi-year plan for future ocean and climate change dialogues, to be called the “Antalya ocean current”. It also asked for the results of these dialogues to be summarised, along with the “best available science” on the ocean, in a synthesis report that would act as an input to the second global stocktake.

However, the cover decision was rejected during the closing plenary. Multiple parties used their interventions during the plenary to express their regret that the work that had been done on the ocean and climate change in the cover text would not move forward.

Pickerell told Carbon Brief that while “it wasn’t a ‘blue COP’ after all”, there were still positive takeaways for the ocean. He said:

“We’ve left with maybe nothing in writing, but I think we have left with genuine momentum. There does seem to be this shared ambition, to move beyond just the recognition of the ocean…There’s lots of opportunities to take this forward.”

Deforestation

COP31 was relatively quiet on forests, compared to last year’s summit in Belém. 

The presidency held a forest leaders’ summit on 11 November, which was attended by the presidents of Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo, along with the prime ministers of the Netherlands and Norway.

Much of the summit dwelled on the Brazil-led Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF).

Delegates speculated that the summit would yield major new pledges for the fund. 

However, only $88m from philanthropies emerged as new contributions at the event. Several countries reiterated past and recent pledges.

At the summit, Jonas Gahr Støre, Norway’s prime minister, said: 

“I am hopeful we can reach our collective goal of mobilising the initial $10bn dollars and to increase from there through next year and, with this, Norway is ready to contribute up to 20% of that total.”

Norway’s “up to $3bn” loan to the fund is conditional upon it hitting the $10bn mark by the end of 2026. At the same time, Støre acknowledged that “it will take some time before payments reach the tropical forest countries and the key people who we want to support”.

This means the fund has – so far – mobilised $8.2bn from different international partners, mostly as conditional loans. This leaves it $1.8bn short of a $10bn target for public and philanthropic capital for this year. 

Political economist Max Alexander Matthey told Carbon Brief that less capital to invest and fewer risks taken will “lead to a fund that will not be able to deliver on the initially promised $4 per hectare” of protected forest in participating countries, even in a best-case scenario. 

Although significant attention was paid to the fossil-fuel roadmap at COP31, far less focus was given to the deforestation one.

Chris Dragisic, managing director for global policy at the National Audubon Society, told Carbon Brief that, nonetheless, there were “a couple of countries” that committed to producing national forest roadmaps. She added:

“Many others have said, ‘we have a national strategy already’, and they’re looking at this really as an option to accelerate progress…What, for me, is the more interesting thing is that the roadmap recatalysed political will across the board for forests, where these had fallen a little bit off the political radar.”

Other forest-related commitments made at COP31 included Bolivia and Indonesia joining the Forest & Climate Leaders’ Partnership and Brazil’s announcement that it is working on an Indigenous peoples’ roadmap.

The COP31 presidency also launched the voluntary “Antalya action plan” on global wildfires, which it said would help a “community of countries” to “cooperate on prevention, early warning, landscape resilience and access to resources”.

On the penultimate scheduled day of the summit, more than 100 organisations – including Indigenous groups, civil society and research institutions – signed an open letter calling on countries to take the work of the deforestation roadmap forward. It also called for an “international convening” on deforestation to occur in 2027.

While an initial draft of the cover text “welcome[d]” the Brazil-led roadmap on deforestation, this was subsequently cut.  

The final cover text – which was rejected during the closing plenary – did retain wording on deforestation agreed by countries in the global stocktake at COP28 in Dubai. The text had also included a recognition of nature-based solutions as “essential climate solutions”, although there is significant controversy over their use.

Methane

Cutting emissions of methane, the potent but short-lived greenhouse gas, appeared to have a renewed push at COP31. 

This is partly due to the recent confirmation of an “inevitable” overshoot of the 1.5C global temperature target. (See: Cover text.) 

 Inger Andersen, chief of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), referred to this at a COP31 methane event: 

“[Methane] leaves the atmosphere quickly, so cutting its emissions is our emergency brake to slow warming.”

It is “one of the fastest, cheapest and most effective ways to check global heating in the near-term”, said UN climate chief Simon Stiell at a 12 November event on non-CO2 greenhouse gases. 

At this event, UNEP announced that its methane alert system has flagged five methane leaks across Canada, Iraq, Kazakhstan and Mexico since June 2026, allowing those countries to mitigate 125,000 tonnes of methane. 

New private funding of $480m (£366m) was also pledged for action on methane and other “super pollutants”.

Nine of the 159 countries who backed a 2021 Global Methane Pledge reaffirmed their aim to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% by 2030 at the event, which was co-hosted by Brazil, China and the UK.

Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Indonesia, Micronesia, Norway, the Netherlands and the UK endorsed this “ministerial declaration”, committing to accelerate action towards the 2030 goal. 

Separately, Australia endorsed a COP30 statement on reducing methane emissions from fossil-fuel production. 

At the beginning of the second week of COP31, Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, launched a petition calling to “reduc[e] methane emissions to near zero”. 

On 11 November, the daily COP31 theme centred on “zero waste”. Emine Erdoğan, the Turkish first lady and chair of a UN advisory board on waste, launched a “global zero waste alliance”.

This aims to “build a strong foundation for cooperation where countries learn from one another” on cutting waste, said Erdoğan at the launch event.

Despite this focus, the Guardian reported before COP31 that Turkey has some of the “world’s worst landfill methane leaks”. 

New climate science

On day one of COP31, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) presented its State of the Climate 2026 update – the latest in its annual series of reports unpacking key climate indicators.

The report finds that 2026 will be one of four warmest years on record. The global average surface temperature for January-September 2026 was about 1.47C above the pre-industrial average, says the report. 

It adds that El Niño is forecast to continue into early 2027, further boosting global temperatures.

At a press conference to launch the report on 9 November, WMO secretary general Prof Celeste Saulo warned that “this 2026-27 El Niño is off the charts”, adding that “it is different from any El Niño that we have monitored”. 

Saulo warned that “we are supercharging our weather” and that “the human and economic cost is unacceptably high”. She continued:

“In 2026, millions of people were exposed to unbearable heat, leading to tens of thousands of excess deaths in Europe alone. India and Pakistan and large parts of Asia and North America suffered dangerous heatwaves. And, as we head into the southern hemisphere summer, we will see more.

“The catastrophe in China and Nepal showed the dangers of high-mountain disasters for downstream communities.”

She concluded with a call to improve early warning systems, stating that “sustained observations from every part of the world are more important than ever”.

The following day, the Global Carbon Project released its latest annual assessment on CO2 emissions and carbon sinks. The 21st edition of the report, written by more than 100 experts from around the world, finds that the world is projected to emit 32.8bn tonnes of CO2 this year, marking a 0.4% decrease compared to 2025.

According to the report, CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and cement are set to fall by around 0.4% in 2026, largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz. (This follows separate analysis by Carbon Brief earlier this year suggesting there would be a 0.5% fall due to the Hormuz crisis.)

Meanwhile, it finds that emissions from coal are continuing to increase slightly.

(For more on the findings, read Carbon Brief’s detailed write-up of the report.)

A subset of the report’s authors also published a study in Nature Climate Change on 10 November, stating that “acceleration in clean technology deployment is needed to guarantee emissions peak and subsequent decline”. 

Another Nature Climate Change paper, published on the opening day of COP31, finds that regions worldwide may have already experienced around 90-94% of the warming expected when the global average reaches 1.5C above pre-industrial levels. 

Food and water

A number of initiatives relating to food and water were launched during COP31.

“Food security” – including transforming agriculture and focusing on water and drought – was one of the priority themes in the COP31 presidency’s “action agenda”. (See: Action agenda.)

Despite this, only a few prominent announcements arrived compared to previous years. 

On 9 November, when the daily COP theme centred on food, agriculture and health, thinktank Clim-Eat launched a report on the reform of agricultural subsidies.

This noted that governments spend approximately $840bn (£638bn) on support and subsidies for agriculture, a sector which majorly contributes to climate change and environmental degradation. 

The report outlined ways to move these subsidies towards payments supporting soil health, public infrastructure and increasing farm incomes in a more targeted way. 

On 10 November, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) launched a platform aimed at helping countries boost alignment in managing food security, water and climate action, called the “turquoise nexus initiative“. 

Led by Turkey, it will exist within the FAO’s “food and agriculture for sustainable transformation” (FAST) partnership, which was launched at COP27 in 2022. 

This is designed to boost climate finance for the transformation of food systems, while also supporting efforts on adaptation and other issues. 

İbrahim Yumaklı, Turkey’s agriculture minister, said the “turquoise” platform would be used to strengthen existing initiatives, rather than create new ones. 

On 11 November, Ethiopia joined a group of eight other nations in the Alliance of Champions for Food Systems Transformation (ACF), a coalition launched at COP28 in 2023. 

This sent a “powerful signal that food systems belong at the heart of climate action”, given that Ethiopia is due to host COP32 next year, said Emma Williams, the head of the ACF secretariat, in a statement.

NDCs

On 27 October, the UNFCCC released its annual report on nationally determined contributions (NDCs). These documents outline countries’ ambitions, as agreed under the Paris Agreement, to limit greenhouse gas emissions up to 2035.

Based on analysis of the latest NDCs, the report says emissions are due to decrease by around 9% by 2035, compared to 2019 levels, if all pledges are implemented – a drop from the 12% reduction estimated in last year’s report.

This leaves countries “substantially off track” to limit global temperatures to 1.5C, the report says.

A small number of countries announced new NDCs around the time of COP31.

Argentina, Botswana, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Egypt, Guatemala, North Macedonia, Palestine and Tajikistan all submitted new pledges in November.

Libya also submitted its first-ever NDC, committing to reducing its carbon emissions per unit of its gross domestic product (GDP) by 28% by 2035.

Protests and access 

Nearly 10,000 people marched through the streets of Antalya on Saturday 14 November, protesting climate change, genocide in Gaza and human-rights abuses in Turkey.

The middle Saturday of COP is the summit’s traditional “protest day”. 

Le Monde reported that Antalya’s protest “stood out for its scale in a country where the space for protest, both environmental and political, is narrow”.

Elsewhere at the summit, Swedish campaigner Greta Thunberg made her first appearance at a UN climate summit since COP26 in Glasgow in 2021. Speaking to a huddle of journalists on 12 November, she said:

“The climate crisis is already here and now – and it is already a matter of life and death. 

“The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.”

She was joined by global-south campaigners, including Mohammed Usrof, a climate activist and researcher from Gaza, who called out countries that continue to supply fossil fuels to Israel, telling journalists:

“Corporations continue to fuel not just genocide in Palestine, but the devastation of the world. [There is a] never-ending proliferation of fossil fuels that we are seeing the consequences all over the global majority world.

“So, it’s extremely crucial here to recognise what is happening in this COP, the stakes that we are here for [and] the stakes that our lived realities essentially symbolise to these negotiations.”

Other speakers alongside Thunberg included Sagar Dhakal, a young Nepalese politician, who said “there are not any words in the dictionary” to describe the catastrophic flash floods in his country earlier this year, in addition to First Nations activist Rikki Dank and Rwanda-DRC activist Celine Isimbi.

COP31 was plagued with logistical problems – particularly during the summit’s opening days – forcing delegates to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to access the venue.

The delays sparked serious access concerns, with the ECO newsletter – a daily bulletin put together by campaigners – writing on 11 November:

“Participation is not a courtesy the presidency gives out when it’s convenient. It is written into the system. Under Article 4.1(i) of the convention, parties committed to encourage ‘the widest participation’ in this process, including by non-governmental organisations. Article 12 of the Paris Agreement calls for public participation and public access to information. Nobody added a footnote saying ‘subject to traffic conditions’.”

During the first part of the final plenary on 20 November, a protester – who was wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” – was ejected after standing on a chair with a red noose around their neck.

Road to COP32 and beyond

At COP30, it was agreed that COP32 in 2027 will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Under the UN’s regional rotational system for hosting COP, the country will be representing the African region.

It will be the first-ever COP hosted by one of the least-developed countries.

Ethiopia’s prime minister Abiy Ahmed addressed the world leaders’ summit at COP31, touting his country’s fossil fuel-free electricity grid and pledging to make finance for developing countries a central part of COP32. He told other leaders: 

“Dependable finance requires cooperation, even as competition between countries grows. Yet, we discuss climate in one room, development in another, trade and finance in two more. Many of us see it in all four. In each of those rooms we should ask how we will finance the future that we have agreed to build.”

(There have been some concerns that conflict in the country might affect its ability to host.)

During the first week of COP31, China ruled out hosting COP33 in 2028, which is due to be held in Asia. (In August, Bloomberg reported that the world’s largest emitter was considering hosting the conference.) India had withdrawn a bid to host COP33 in April.

Countries that are considering making a bid to host COP33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand, according to the Guardian.

item.dc:creator: Simon Evans
item.description:
Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon…

The post Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time appeared first on Carbon Brief.
item.content:encoded:
Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.

Since 1850, the three nations – and other major fossil-fuel exporters – have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 in the form of gas, oil and coal that has been burned in other countries.

Carbon Brief’s analysis of extraction-based CO2 emissions is based on figures compiled by Robbie Andrew, a senior researcher at Norwegian climate institute CICERO.

It shows that Australia is responsible for more than twice as much global warming when including emissions from its fossil-fuel exports, while Saudi Arabia has caused more than four times as much.

Australia has been under pressure for continuing to expand its fossil-fuel production ahead of the UN climate summit in Antalya, where it is co-president with host nation Turkey.

Membership

Connect with our community

Join CB+

In contrast, nations that are heavily reliant on energy imports – such as Japan or Germany – are responsible for far lower shares of planet-warming emissions, if responsibility passes to fossil-fuel producers.

There are many different ways to assign historical responsibility for current global warming.

Carbon Brief has previously published analysis based on territorial emissions, the consumption of imported goods, according to colonial rule or based on historical emissions per capita.

Historical responsibility

This year is expected to be around 1.5C hotter than pre-industrial temperatures. Next year is forecast to be the hottest on record, at around 1.7C of warming.

This year-to-year variation is due to natural variability, such as El Niño. However, approximately 100% of global warming to date is the result of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

The burning of fossil fuels since the industrial revolution is the largest contributor to this.

Since there is a direct link between each tonne of CO2 and each fraction of a degree of warming, historical fossil-fuel emissions can be tied to responsibility for current climate change.

This is typically calculated on the basis of historical territorial CO2 emissions, according to where in the world the fossil fuels are burned. It is also possible to assign historical responsibility on a “consumption” basis, according to where goods are used.

Historical emissions are often counted by country, but this puts the focus on populous nations. Alternatively, responsibility can be assigned per capita, based on today’s populations.

A less-familiar way to look at the question of historical responsibility is to consider where fossil fuels are extracted. This puts the spotlight on major fossil-fuel exporters.

The figure below shows that Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the largest CO2 exporters of all time, based on emissions from exported fossil fuels since 1850.

(The allocation is based on extraction taking place within current national borders. Emissions under the former USSR, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia are allocated among constituent countries, based on their share of emissions at the time of separation.)

Other major CO2 exporters, based on their overseas sales of fossil fuels since 1850, include Venezuela, Iran, Norway, the United Arab Emirates and Canada.

Between them, these major coal, oil and gas producers have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 over the past 175 years, according to Carbon Brief’s analysis.

Extraction-based accounting

The analysis shows that overall, the US and China retain the largest responsibility for historical warming under extraction-based accounting, despite having been net CO2 importers since 1850.

The US has large resources of coal, oil and gas, but was nevertheless a major oil importer until after the shale revolution in the early 2000s.

China remains a major oil and gas importer, describing itself as “rich in coal, lacking oil and gas”.

Russia remains in third place, as shown in the figure below, despite gaining responsibility for an extra 69bn tonnes of CO2 from exported fossil fuels.

The UK becomes the fourth-largest historical emitter, climbing above Germany due to the latter’s reliance on fossil-fuel imports.

Saudi Arabia becomes responsible for the world’s fifth-largest share of historical warming when including its fossil-fuel exports, which increase its cumulative emissions more than fourfold.

Australia also climbs up the rankings, becoming one of the top-ten largest emitters when including its fossil-fuel exports. This more than doubles its share of historical emissions.

Nations that drop down the rankings under extraction-based accounting, due to their reliance on fossil-fuel imports, include Germany, India, France and COP31 host Turkey.

Japan is a particularly notable example, as it is almost completely reliant on fossil-fuel imports. The nation is the sixth-largest emitter on a territorial basis and the 34th-largest on an extraction basis.

Per-capita accounting

When considering population sizes, major fossil-fuel exporters have the highest extraction-based CO2 emissions since 1850, as shown in the figure below.

Small nations that export large amounts of oil and gas are particularly prominent on this list, including Brunei, Kuwait, Qatar, Norway and Trinidad and Tobago.

Andrew tells Carbon Brief that while the extraction-based accounting offers an alternative perspective on historical responsibility for warming, it also raises complex questions. He explains: 

“At the end of the day, it’s not solely the responsibility of extracting countries that fuels are combusted; it’s joint responsibility between extractors, producers and consumers.”

He adds that responsibility for past decisions is shared by many actors. For example, he notes that oil production in the Middle East was historically “developed by and for western powers”.

About the data

National emissions under extraction-based accounting come from a dataset developed by Robbie Andrew and covering the period from 1850-2025.

Emissions are allocated to the country that extracted the relevant fossil fuels, regardless of where the coal, oil or gas was burned.

The allocation is based on current national borders. Emissions that took place within the former USSR, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia are allocated among their present-day constituent countries, based on the relative shares of emissions at the time of separation.

Andrew notes that the dataset is a draft release, based on available data.

Population data for 2025 is taken from the UN Population Fund.

item.title: COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions
item.dc:creator: Simon Evans
item.description:
UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to…

The post COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions appeared first on Carbon Brief.
item.content:encoded:
UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions. 

Carbon Brief readers submitted questions via CB Connect on topics including the UK’s “climate leadership”, the COP31 electrification target, as well as the roadmaps on deforestation and fossil fuels.  

Despite recent criticism over the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, Miliband argued that the UK is still seen as a climate leader, due to its “ambitious targets on net-zero”. 

COP31 coverage

  • COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya
  • Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’?

  • COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya

  • Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?
  • Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit
  • Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit

Pushing back on a question about COP reform, Miliband explained how he is “quite pro the institution of the COP”, given its role in bringing countries together for climate action. 

He emphasised the importance of action on methane and the UK’s “support” for the “35×35” electrification pledge. 

Carbon Brief: Well, thanks very much for joining us. I know you’re very busy and we’ve got some reader questions. It’s great that you’ve got time to answer some.

Ed Miliband: Can I just say how much I love Carbon Brief?

CB: Thanks. Lovely to hear.

EM: Like, comment and subscribe!

CB: How, in your experience at COP31 so far, has the UK’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field and the rumoured rollback of its EV targets affected the UK’s standing as a climate leader?

EM: People see us as showing leadership. People don’t see us as rolling back, and I think what people see is a government that is driving the agenda on electrification and clean power. Because after all, we have a clean power 2030 target, which is world-leading. 

[We] have the most ambitious targets on net-zero, the [nationally determined contributions] NDCs, of frankly, any country in the world. [We] are legislating for no new oil and gas licences. 

And what I’m trying to do here is also bring a new dimension to this, which is the whole national security dimension. Because I think, if you’re serious about national security, you need to be serious about climate. And those parties – and those people – who aren’t serious about climate, I don’t think they’re serious about national security. Because this is a national security issue for, I think – frankly – every government across the world.

So I think, look, people see British leadership. People are looking forward to our [presidency of the] G20 [in 2027], where climate resilience [and] debt development will be central to the agenda as well. 

CB: Are you confident that the UK can still meet its 2030 NDC target [to cut emissions 68% below 1990 levels]?

EM: Absolutely, we’re going to go all out to meet it. I think that’s so important, and that is the whole principle of the NDCs, is [that] you drive towards seeking to meet them. Obviously, it’s stretching. We inherited, from 2024, a difficult situation from the previous government, but we’re going to go all out to do what we can.

Membership

Connect with our community

Join CB+

CB: Great. With the UK and other developed countries facing increasing fiscal pressures, how can you go about ensuring developing countries receive the financial and technical support that they need?

EM: Look, I think the biggest thing we need to do, cognisant of those fiscal pressures and the situation facing developing countries, is multilateral development bank (MDB) reform. So making sure that the MDBs work to the maximum for developing countries.

There’s lots of evidence out there and I was speaking about this at the World Bank annual meetings about the fact that the MDBs could do more to leverage their balance sheets. You know, potentially hundreds of billions of pounds – dollars – more that could be helping developing countries. Helping developing countries with climate resilience, helping them with relieving the debt burden in terms of the financing of the debt.

And, you know, one of the things that we’re going to be doing as part of our G20 is convening those MDBs to, in a friendly way, you know, point to the best practice of some of them, push the others to do more. I feel from our discussions that this is absolutely possible – for us to do more.

So yes, there are more fiscal constraints in developed countries, including in Britain, but it doesn’t mean we can’t make a difference. And I think it’s really, really important to say to your viewers: we are serious about, not just our national leadership on climate, but our international leadership as well, and we believe we can make a difference.

CB: It’s become part of the narrative that the COP process has run its course, and that people should focus more on mini-coalitions, groups of middle powers. What would you say to that, and how would you like to see the COP process reformed?

EM: I mean, I’m quite pro the COP process – not the process, but I’m quite pro the institution of the COP – and I’d say that in two respects. 

One, if you look at the sweep of history, I was at the Copenhagen COP of 2009, [which] ended in acrimony. We were heading for a 4C world back then. Now, we’re heading for a 2.5C, 2.6C world, according to the latest UNEP emissions gap report – one of my favourite publications. 

And look, 2.6C is bad, right? And we’ve got to do a lot more as a world, but we have made progress. And why? Because of multilateralism, because of the institution, being part of the COP, driving people forward. 

That’s one part of it. The second part of it is [that the COP is] a place where these “coalitions of the willing” are formed. If I think about what I’ve done while I’ve been here [in Antalya] – I was at an event on forests, coalitions of the willing acting on the forest leaders’ partnership, acting to protect the forest. An event on electrification, a big focus of the Turkish presidency. An event on industrial policy, green industrial policy. Countries working together. An event this morning on methane, really crucial. We’re trying to, with a coalition of the willing, get it onto the COP agenda. And then, an event on climate security. 

So that gives people, your viewers, a sense of why I think this [COP process] matters. You know, it’s not simply a talking shop. I think it is also a place where action happens. 

CB: You mentioned the electrification pledge put forward by the Turkish presidency. Is the UK a signatory to that yet? 

EM: We support the electrification pledge, absolutely, and you know we want to drive forward. It’s stretching for the UK, but we think it’s the right thing to do. And why? Because – it’s really important to say this – because electrification is a way of getting off the fossil-fuel rollercoaster. Clean-energy electrification is the way I think about it.

[Three hours after Carbon Brief’s interview with Ed Miliband, the UK government confirmed its endorsement of the 35×35 electrification pledge.]

And if there’s one lesson we’ve got to learn from these two wars that we’ve seen – Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran war – it’s [that] you can’t have security on the basis of fossil fuels. It’s not even – even [for a] country like America, a massive fossil-fuel producer is affected by higher prices. But for fossil-fuel importers, covering 75% of the world’s population [including the UK], we are price takers. And you know the fossil-fuel rollercoaster is terrible for the cost of living. That’s why clean energy, clean electrification, is the answer. Electrify now!

CB: The UN climate convention and the Paris Agreement both commit countries, including the UK, to implement “climate-change education, training, public awareness and participation”. Why doesn’t the UK have a national programme on this, particularly given the flood of misinformation in this area?

EM: We need to do more. You’re completely right. Look, I am always ambitious to do more, and more climate education – well, more public information – is important. 

I did the first annual climate and nature statement in 2025. It was repeated in 2026 by [environment secretary] Mary Creagh. I was in the House of Commons for that, and that whole institution was part of me believing, as energy secretary, that it was important to find ways to inform the public. 

And I fully acknowledge we need to do more. We need to do more. But we need to do more to both tell people about what is happening, in terms of climate and nature, but also say there are answers, because it can’t just be a council of despair. It’s also got to be a council of hope – not false hope – but a council of honesty, but also hope. 

CB: Great. How would you like to see the Brazilian roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation taken forward? Are you keen to see those as part of the formal negotiated outcome [at COP31]? 

EM: I think what’s interesting about this goes back to your question about the coalition of the willing. Look, there’s obviously no secret that there are countries that are obstacles to the fossil-fuel roadmap being part of – central – to the COP decision. And we took a decision last year that there was a big enough coalition of the willing – I think there are 80 countries or more – to drive this forward.

I think the Brazilians are to be incredibly commended for having produced this fossil-fuel roadmap. I think we should now be thinking, as individual countries, how can we build on that work ourselves? Because it’s doing exactly what I hoped it would do, which is to grapple with the important issues that we face.

I think we have to accept there are some countries – in a world where you have to operate by consensus – where not every decision is going to get into the COP decision. But it doesn’t mean we can’t make progress on it, and I think that’s really true in this case.

CB: Great. One final question from my end, if I may. What’s an outcome that you’re going to be looking for at the end of this COP, that you’re going to be happy to take home to the UK? 

EM: I think the most important thing is action to drive forward the climate agenda, and that’s what I want to see. You know, it goes back to the point about the cost. Some of it is about the formal decision-making, but a lot of it is about the real, tangible outcomes that have happened over a couple of weeks.

And if I think about what I’ve done here, you know, if we can get methane and the importance of methane – which, as you know, and as your viewers will know – is such an important short-term difference we can make in terms of preventing the rise in temperatures, and we can get that onto the agenda of the COP. If we can show progress on other aspects of the real economy – what’s happening in the real economy – all of those things are going to be important.

I think there’s something else, though, which is, these events of countries coming together. They contradict those people who say, you know, people are giving up on climate. Because you’ve got more than 190 countries that are coming together [at the COP], reaffirming their belief in the Paris Agreement, reaffirming their belief that they need to make efforts, as part of the Paris Agreement, to meet the climate goals – and working together on these issues. 

It doesn’t mean they aren’t hard, but it does show that there is really important global commitment, which I’ve been hearing, to this agenda.

CB: Brilliant. Thanks very much, Ed.

EM: Thank you. 

This interview was conducted by Dr Simon Evans at the COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, on 12 November 2026. Filming by Josh Gabbatiss and Daisy Dunne, with editing by Joe Goodman.

item.title: Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31
item.dc:creator: Josh Gabbatiss
item.description:
The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in…

The post Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31  appeared first on Carbon Brief.
item.content:encoded:
The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.

Developed countries are required under UN climate treaties to provide “climate finance” and have traditionally announced multi-year pledges to feed into their global commitments.

Most of these pledges expired in 2025 and, since then, the US has withdrawn from international climate efforts and many European aid budgets have been cut.

COP31 coverage

  • COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya
  • Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’?
  • CB Live: Carbon Brief journalists discuss key COP31 outcomes
  • COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya
  • COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions
  • Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31?
  • Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?
  • Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit
  • Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit

A civil-society tracker shows that only six nations have announced new multi-year pledges, including just one major donor – the UK.

Germany, France and Japan are among the key contributors that have so far failed to set out plans for new climate finance, while none is expected from the US.

As a result, the total amount of public climate finance pledged over the next few years amounts to just $11.7bn a year in spending, down from recent levels of around $40bn.

Experts tell Carbon Brief that global conflict, fiscal constraints and the rise of the far right are all making it harder for developed-country governments to pledge new funds.

As the COP31 summit in Turkey gets underway, developing countries are stressing their urgent need for new finance, after nations agreed to a new global target just two years ago.

Missing pledges

Under the Paris Agreement, developed countries are obliged to provide climate finance to help developing countries cut their emissions and prepare for climate disasters.

This financial assistance can be channelled through multilateral development banks, UN climate funds and investments “mobilised” from the private sector.

But a large chunk is also expected to come directly from the public coffers of developed countries – primarily their foreign-aid budgets. This public spending has made up roughly a third of climate finance flowing to developing countries in recent years.

The EU, the US and others agreed just two years ago that they would “take the lead” on scaling up annual climate finance from $100bn in the early 2020s to $300bn by 2035.

Donor countries have traditionally supported such goals by announcing multi-year targets that indicate how much they plan to spend on climate finance.

Nearly all of these pledges expired in 2025 – and hardly any major donors have announced new ones to replace them, covering the period out to 2030. 

This lack of new commitments is captured in a tracker of old and new financial commitments by climate NGOs NRDC and E3G.

Carbon Brief analysis of this data, based on an annualised breakdown of targets, shows that developed countries had previously pledged around £42bn a year in public finance. 

As the chart below shows, based on current pledges, this has fallen by around 71% to £11.8bn, on average, over the remainder of the 2020s.

Not all contributors announced public climate-finance pledges in advance for the pre-2026 period. Some did not hit their stated targets, while others exceeded them.

While official data for 2025 is not yet available, bilateral public finance reached £43.9bn in 2024, broadly in line with the amount pledged by developed countries.

Big contributors

International climate finance has been consistently dominated by five nations – Japan, Germany, France, the US and the UK.

These countries – together with the EU – have provided around 90% of all the bilateral, public climate finance going to developing countries in recent years.

Of these key players, only the UK has announced a new pledge, committing £6bn ($8bn) of aid between 2026-27 and 2028-29, plus £6.7bn ($8.9bn) from outside its aid budget.

This accounts for half of all the annual funds pledged from 2026 onwards – averaging $5.7bn a year.

The European Commission makes up most of the remainder, with an average annual contribution of $4.5bn promised out to 2027. 

Rather than a new pledge, this is due to the commission promising to spend €28bn ($31.8bn) over its 2021-2027 budget period. Its post-2027 contribution is currently being discussed as part of wider EU budget negotiations.

Canada has promised to spend CA$5.3bn ($4.1bn) by 2030, averaging $860m a year. The Netherlands, Switzerland, Belgium and Luxembourg have also pledged relatively small sums.

Overall, despite developed countries committing to scale up climate finance, these new pledges are either less ambitious – or only slightly more ambitious – than previous ones. This can be seen in the chart below.

The UK’s pledge appears more ambitious, but this is because the government has changed how it counts climate finance to include $8.9bn in “additional” public finance. When only the like-for-like aid components are compared, the new pledge amounts to a drop in ambition. (For more details, see the methodology.)

The most significant absence is the US, which committed to reaching $11.4bn in annual support by 2024 under the Biden administration.

Since president Donald Trump took power, the US has – for the second time – withdrawn from the Paris Agreement and shrunk its aid budget. It will not provide any official climate finance in the coming years.

Another notable absence is Australia, which is jointly hosting the upcoming COP31 summit, alongside Turkey. Josie Lee, policy and advocacy lead at Oxfam Australia, tells Carbon Brief:

“If Australia fails to announce a climate-finance pledge as president of negotiations, it would send a problematic message to those resisting action on climate change that might serve to embolden their agenda.”

Japan is the largest overall contributor of public climate finance, but it has not traditionally announced targets for this type of spending. Instead, the government set out overall goals that also bundle in finance “mobilised” from the private sector.

As a result, its public-finance ambitions have not been included in this analysis.

So far, the Japanese government has not announced any new multi-year climate-finance pledges, from either the public or the private sector.

European cuts

Europe provides the majority of international climate finance, but European governments have massively cut their aid spending in recent years, citing economic strain and defence spending needs.

Germany and France, the two largest European climate-finance contributors, both pledged to reach €6bn ($6.8bn) per year by 2025. Neither has committed to anything beyond that. 

Both nations have slashed their aid budgets in recent years, including funding for climate programmes. Germany missed its 2025 climate-finance goal due to these cuts.

Dr Anja Carolin Gebel, a senior policy advisor at Germanwatch, tells Carbon Brief that this issue has become more politically fraught since the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) won the 2025 election and began leading a coalition government:

“The issue of climate change – and, subsequently, climate finance – has taken a back seat in the current government coalition.”

There has also been a political shift in France, Gaïa Febvre, international policy coordinator at Réseau Action Climat, tells Carbon Brief. She adds:

“The upcoming presidential election and the growing influence of the far right are likely to make new international financial commitments politically more difficult.”

Other significant European donors are also undergoing political turmoil. 

Spain’s centre-left government has triggered a snap election for the end of November, making a new climate-finance pledge during COP31 less likely.

Following a narrow election win, a centre-left bloc in Sweden is still in the process of trying to form a new coalition government.

Some nations have signalled that their climate finance will continue flowing, even though they have not officially set out specific new pledges. 

The Dutch government, for example, has said it will provide “at least” €300m ($334m) of specific climate funding annually out to 2031. However, it has also indicated that its total public climate finance is likely to be considerably higher in both 2026 and 2027.

To highlight the lack of new pledges, developing countries are championing a “climate-finance work programme” at COP31, which could provide a space to discuss scaling up public climate finance from developed countries.

In response, the EU has stressed that its member states are the “largest providers” of public climate finance and called on developing countries to submit overdue plans for cutting emissions. The EU and its member states provided a record €32.3bn ($40bn) in 2025.

Membership

Connect with our community

Join CB+

Against this backdrop, EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra recently told Bloomberg that “any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water”.

Joe Thwaites, international climate finance director at NRDC, who runs the commitment tracker, tells Carbon Brief that “developed countries would be wise to show how they are continuing to lead on climate finance”. He says:

“The lack of new announcements is making the finance negotiations tougher than they need to be. The debate around the climate-finance work programme is arising because developing countries have little clarity about how much public climate finance there will be in coming years.”

Update: This piece has been updated to include a pledge for the 2026-2030 period from Luxembourg.

Methodology

This analysis is based on the climate-finance commitments tracker, run by the NGOs NRDC and E3G, supplemented with additional research.

Only the 23 “developed” countries that are obliged to provide climate finance are considered in this analysis, plus the EU. This includes western Europe, the US, Australia, Canada and New Zealand. Japan and Norway both provide substantial sums of climate finance, but have not announced specific public-finance pledges and therefore are not included.

Carbon Brief converted multi-year pledges into single years, with 2025 used as the baseline “pre-2026” year. Some countries committed to reaching a certain amount “by 2025”, in which case that value is used. Others said they would provide a total amount over several years, in which case the average value per year is used. Belgium, Switzerland and the US only set initial targets as far as 2024, so their 2024 values were used instead of 2025.

These values were compared with the average annual contribution for the remainder of the 2020s, based on the new pledges from the UK, Canada, Belgium, Switzerland and the Netherlands. Some climate finance has been committed by the Netherlands, but this is not expected to be its total contribution. The EU, Portugal and Greece have earlier pledges that extend into the latter half of the 2020s, although the latter two make very small contributions.

NRDC and E3G include all the UK’s newly pledged public finance in their tracker, including $8.9bn in “additional” public finance, which covers “equity, debt, guarantees, insurance and export credit” to mobilise private finance.

In previous Carbon Brief analysis comparing the UK’s new climate-finance target to its old one, this funding was not included. This is because the government did not previously count these funds towards its climate-finance goals, instead focusing exclusively on aid spending.

This analysis does not include pledges that some countries, including Germany and France, have made to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). However, these pledges would not substantially change the main finding, shifting the overall reduction from 71% to 70%.
